items.prompt: Which of these is a trait statement?
choices: You skipped Tuesday's design review
You are not much of a team player
The build failed after your merge
items.explanation: A trait labels the person. The other two describe events.

items.prompt: Which of these describes an observable behavior?
choices: You joined standup 15 minutes late on Monday
You clearly do not value the team's time or work
You are generally a bit careless about how things run
items.explanation: Only the first could have been recorded by a camera.

items.prompt: Why can't a report act on 'be more proactive'?
choices: It is always said in a rather unkind tone of voice
It is only ever said during annual performance reviews
It names no specific action to change
items.explanation: A conclusion with no events attached gives nothing to repeat or change.

items.prompt: 'You're disorganized' is best described as what?
choices: A description of one event
A statement of concrete impact
A conclusion about the person
items.explanation: It sums up many events into one label.

items.prompt: Which wording is easier to check as true or false?
choices: You missed the 10am handoff on Friday
You never really follow through on things
You don't seem very reliable lately
items.explanation: A dated event can be confirmed or corrected; impressions cannot.

items.prompt: Trait labels tend to land as what?
choices: A neutral fact about one single moment in time
A judgment about who the person is
A helpful pointer to the next steps to take
items.explanation: Because they describe identity, they read as a verdict.

items.prompt: What can a person actually change by Monday?
choices: What they do in a given situation
What kind of person they are
What their manager thinks of them
items.explanation: Behaviors are changeable; traits and opinions are not a to-do item.

items.prompt: 'Be more of a leader' is missing what?
choices: A friendly tone of voice when it is said
A reference to the company values and culture
A concrete action to take
items.explanation: It is a trait goal with no observable behavior behind it.

items.prompt: Four managers each rewrite 'he is careless in code reviews.' Which rewrite describes a behavior rather than a label or a motive?
choices: Your reviews show a lack of attention to the finer points of detail
You tend to rush reviews whenever you are busy with your own work
On the pricing PR you approved within two minutes with no comments
You clearly do not take other people's code seriously enough at all
items.explanation: Only the first names a checkable event. The others are a trait, a pattern assumption and a guess at motive.
items.reference:
Trait vs. behavior
trait: 'not proactive', a conclusion
behavior: 'no blocker update in Tuesday's standup', observable
only a behavior can be changed on Monday
Why: a trait sums events into a label and throws the events away, so the receiver has nothing concrete to change.
items.learnMore:
Traits versus behaviors

A trait is the conclusion you drew; a behavior is the evidence a camera could have recorded. Feedback that hands over only the conclusion leaves the receiver guessing which evidence produced it.

Common mistake

Softening a trait ('you could be a bit more proactive') and thinking it became specific. It is still a label.
items.reflection: Think of the last vague label someone gave you (or you gave someone). What specific event was hiding behind it?

items.prompt: A report asks, 'You said I'm disorganized, so what should I change?' What does that question reveal about the original feedback?
choices: The report is being defensive and avoiding responsibility for the issue
The manager should have chosen a softer word than disorganized there
The feedback needed to come with a written improvement plan attached
The label kept the verdict but dropped the events behind it
items.explanation: A trait label cannot be unpacked. The receiver has no way to recover which events earned it.

items.prompt: What does the S in SBI stand for?
choices: Situation
Summary
Standards
items.explanation: SBI is Situation-Behavior-Impact.

items.prompt: Which part of SBI describes what happened as a result?
choices: Situation
Behavior
Impact
items.explanation: Impact is the concrete effect of the behavior.

items.prompt: Which part names the observable action?
choices: Impact
Situation
Behavior
items.explanation: Behavior is what was visibly done or said.

items.prompt: Which belongs in the Situation?
choices: In yesterday's 9:15 standup
You seemed uninterested again
It made the team lose time
items.explanation: The Situation names the specific moment.

items.prompt: Which belongs in the Impact?
choices: You joined late to the call that day
We planned the week around a wrong date
In Tuesday's planning session with the team
items.explanation: Impact is the effect, not the action or the moment.

items.prompt: SBI leaves out which of these on purpose?
choices: Guesses about motive
The date on which the event happened
The effect on the team afterward
items.explanation: Motive cannot be observed and invites an argument about intent.

items.prompt: Which is a motive guess that SBI avoids?
choices: You did not mention it in the standup meeting
We replanned two days of work because of it
You didn't care enough to mention it
items.explanation: 'Didn't care' claims to know what is inside the person's head.

items.prompt: What should the receiver be left with after SBI?
choices: A general sense of being watched at all times
A specific thing to repeat or change
A full list of their personality flaws and faults
items.explanation: That is the purpose of the structure.

items.prompt: A manager says: 'In Monday's retro (S) you rolled your eyes when Sam spoke (B), which shows you don't respect him.' What is wrong?
choices: The closing clause guesses at motive instead of stating a real effect
The Situation is too recent to be useful as feedback at this point
The Behavior should have been described in a more gentle way first
A retro is simply the wrong setting for this kind of message at all
items.explanation: Impact must be a real consequence. 'Shows you don't respect him' is an interpretation of motive.
items.reference:
The three parts of SBI
S: the specific moment ('yesterday's 9:15 standup')
B: the observable action ('did not mention the API delay')
I: the concrete effect ('we planned around a wrong date')
Why: each part narrows from where it happened, to what was done, to what it caused, leaving no room for labels or motive guesses.
items.learnMore:
Situation, Behavior, Impact

SBI gives the receiver a moment to recall, an action to examine and a consequence to care about. It deliberately leaves out labels and guesses about motive, since neither can be observed.

Common mistake

Putting a motive inside the Behavior ('you ignored the blocker because you don't care'). That is a guess, not an observation.
items.reflection: Pick a moment from this week when someone's action affected you. Can you state the situation, the action and the effect separately?

items.prompt: Which message contains all three of S, B and I?
choices: On Thursday you did a great job on the incident and the team really noticed it
In Thursday's call you listed rollback steps unprompted, so the revert took ten minutes
You listed rollback steps unprompted, which is how a careful engineer always works
During Thursday's call you were well prepared, and I really appreciated that a lot
items.explanation: Only the first has a moment, an action and a measurable effect. The others have a verdict or a feeling.

choices: About 37%
About 5%
About 87%
items.explanation: 100 times e to the minus one-seventh is about 87.

items.prompt: Roughly how much is retained after three weeks in the model?
choices: About 65%
About 37%
About 5%
items.explanation: At day 21 the model gives about 5%.

items.prompt: Which part of SBI blurs first with delay?
choices: Situation
Impact
The manager's tone
items.explanation: It is the most single-instance detail.

items.prompt: Delayed feedback tends to fall back on what?
choices: Precise quotes from the meeting itself
General statements like 'you're often late'
Exact times and the attendees of it
items.explanation: Without the moment, only a pattern impression remains.

items.prompt: Is the decay curve in the demo a real measurement?
choices: No, it is an illustrative model
Yes, it comes from a large survey of managers
Yes, it was measured carefully in a lab
items.explanation: The unit labels it as a teaching model.

items.prompt: What shortens the gap that causes the fade?
choices: Waiting for the next scheduled quarterly review
Saving up several issues for one longer talk
Giving feedback within a day or two
items.explanation: Fresh delivery preserves the Situation.

items.prompt: Where does the model drop fastest?
choices: Between day 20 and day 30
In the first few days
Exactly at day 14
items.explanation: An exponential decay is steepest at the start.

items.prompt: Quarterly reviews are a weak place for incident feedback because...
choices: managers are usually too busy to attend them at all
the specific moment has faded for both people
reports are never allowed to reply in them
items.explanation: Neither person can reconstruct the event.

items.prompt: A manager gives well-structured SBI feedback twenty-one days late, with no notes. In the unit's model, what has most likely happened?
choices: The Impact has become more serious because it has had time to grow bigger
The Behavior has been replaced by a trait label in the receiver's own mind
Nothing important, because a clear structure protects against memory loss
The Situation has faded into a guess such as 'you're often late'
items.explanation: The Situation is what decays first; structure cannot fix a missing moment.
items.reference:
Specifics fade fast (modeled)
day 1: 87% of specifics retrievable
day 7: 37%
day 21: 5%
the Situation goes first
Why: the Situation is the most single-instance detail, so it blurs first, and what is left is a pattern-level trait statement.
items.learnMore:
Why delay erodes the S

The unit's demo models retained specificity as exponential decay with a seven-day time constant. The numbers are illustrative, not measured, but the shape (a steep early drop) is the point.

Common mistake

Thinking a good memory fixes it. The fix is a shorter gap, or notes written the same day.

items.prompt: How many independent dials does good feedback need?
choices: Two: timing and content
One: timing alone is enough for it
One: tone is the only thing that matters
items.explanation: Both must be set well.

items.prompt: Feedback arrives the same afternoon: 'You need to be a better communicator.' What has timing fixed?
choices: The Situation, which is now fresh enough to be quoted in full
Nothing, because there was no specific moment to preserve

The Impact, which is always easiest to see on the same day it happens
items.explanation: Freshness only preserves details that were included.
items.reference:
Two dials: speed and specificity
fast + specific: best case
fast + vague: vagueness delivered sooner
slow + specific: specifics have faded
slow + vague: worst case
Why: speed protects the Situation but only structure supplies Behavior and Impact; neither rescues the other.
items.learnMore:
Timing and content are independent

A grid of fast/slow and specific/vague shows four different outcomes. Feedback that is quick but trait-based can even send the receiver in the wrong direction.

Common mistake

Believing that 'telling them right away' is the whole job. Speed with no structure just delivers confusion sooner.

items.prompt: A manager says 'great leadership in the incident.' Which rewrite keeps the praise but makes it SBI?
choices: During Tuesday's outage you showed real leadership and a great deal of calm
Tuesday's outage went well overall, partly thanks to your leadership skills

items.explanation: Only the first has a moment, a behavior and an effect. The rest keep the verdict.
items.reference:
Praise needs the same structure
'Great job' → a mood, nothing to repeat
S-B-I praise → the exact habit to keep
specific praise is also harder to fake
Why: a positive trait label is as vague as a negative one; naming the moment, action and effect reinforces a repeatable behavior.
items.learnMore:
SBI for positive feedback

The structure is neutral about direction. Naming what was done and what it caused tells the person which habit to keep, and it reads as believable because it could only be said by someone who noticed.

Common mistake

Saving SBI for problems and praising in generalities. People then learn what to stop but never what to repeat.
items.reflection: What is one specific thing a colleague did recently that you could thank them for using all three parts?

Vague praise lacks any connection to pay or promotion decisions
items.explanation: A pleasant verdict gives a mood, not a habit to keep.

SBI for positive feedback

The structure is neutral about direction. Naming what was done and what it caused tells the person which habit to keep, and it reads as believable because it could only be said by someone who noticed.

Common mistake

Saving SBI for problems and praising in generalities. People then learn what to stop but never what to repeat.
items.reflection: What is one specific thing a colleague did recently that you could thank them for using all three parts?

items.prompt: Which situation shows the decision flow (can you name the moment, action and effect?) correctly stopping a message?
choices: The manager recalls an instance but doubts that the person will care
The manager has three clear instances but is feeling quite busy today
The manager can name the moment and the effect but not the cause
The manager has only a general feeling and cannot recall a single instance
items.explanation: Without a nameable moment, the manager should observe or recall more before saying anything.
items.reference:
Praise needs the same structure
'Great job' → a mood, nothing to repeat
S-B-I praise → the exact habit to keep
specific praise is also harder to fake
Why: a positive trait label is as vague as a negative one; naming the moment, action and effect reinforces a repeatable behavior.

items.prompt: Which version named a Situation, Behavior and Impact?
choices: Version 1
Version 3
Version 2
items.explanation: Only Version 3 is SBI.

items.prompt: Version 1 was delivered when?
choices: About three weeks later
The next day
During the incident itself
items.explanation: It was saved for the quarterly review.

items.prompt: Version 2 is best described as...
choices: Slow but specific
Slow and a trait too
Fast but still a trait
items.explanation: It arrived within the week but said 'quiet'.

items.prompt: What did Version 3 end with?
choices: A warning about the next review
A single specific request
A general encouragement
items.explanation: It asked that flagged items also be said in standup.

items.prompt: The Impact in Version 3 was...
choices: A lost client account
Two days of replanning
A missed holiday weekend
items.explanation: The team planned around a wrong date.

items.prompt: Did Version 3 guess why Priya acted?
choices: No, it described and then asked
Yes, it assumed she was careless
Yes, it assumed she was shy
items.explanation: It stayed with observable facts.

items.prompt: Version 2 might lead Priya to...
choices: correct the exact blocker update
ask for a transfer to another team
talk more in general without fixing the gap
items.explanation: The real gap was not named.

items.prompt: Which Behavior was named in Version 3?
choices: She was often disengaged from the team
She avoided the manager after Tuesday
She did not mention the delay in standup
items.explanation: It named a missing sentence in a specific meeting.

items.prompt: Which element is present in Version 3 but missing from Versions 1 and 2?
choices: A polite opening that asked permission before sharing something with her
A concrete effect with a size attached, two days of replanning
A reference to the quarterly review cycle and how it is scheduled
A broader comment on the team's overall communication culture
items.explanation: Neither earlier version stated any Impact.
items.reference:
One incident, three versions
V1: trait, three weeks later: nothing named
V2: trait, same week: only 'quiet'
V3: SBI, next day: moment, action, effect, request
Why: the same facts produce three different outcomes depending on whether the message names a moment, an action and an effect.
items.learnMore:
Reading the three versions

Version 3 ends with a single specific request. It also avoids diagnosing why the person acted as they did; it describes and then asks.

Common mistake

Adding 'because you probably assumed...' to the Behavior. That is a motive guess dressed as context.
items.reflection: If you had to give feedback on a recent event, which of the three versions would your first draft resemble?

items.prompt: Version 3 asks Priya to say flagged blockers out loud in standup. Why is that a stronger ending than 'try to be more proactive'?
choices: It is longer, so Priya will find it much harder to forget it
It gives Priya a way to avoid private conversations in future
It is one action she can do and the manager can later observe
It is kinder because it never mentions the manager's concerns
items.explanation: A repeatable action is checkable; 'proactive' is a label.

items.prompt: Which phrase keeps a pattern conversation checkable?
choices: The 3rd, the 10th and the 17th
This keeps happening again and again
You always do this to us, every time
items.explanation: Dated instances can be confirmed.

items.prompt: Why is 'you always...' a poor opener?
choices: It is too short to sound polite
It is only meant for use in team settings
It cannot be checked and invites an argument
items.explanation: People argue about 'always' instead of the events.

items.prompt: What does waiting through several instances do?
choices: Makes the issue fix itself over time
Builds frustration that lands as criticism
Makes the later feedback much shorter to say
items.explanation: The eventual message becomes a pile.

items.prompt: What goes first when describing a pattern?
choices: A character summary
Each dated instance
A comparison to coworkers
items.explanation: Instances are the evidence.

items.prompt: If only one instance can be named clearly, the honest message is about...
choices: that one instance
a pattern anyway
the person's reliability
items.explanation: Do not stretch one event into a trend.

items.prompt: After listing instances, which step comes next in the flow?
choices: Announce the review rating that follows
Switch to praise only for the rest of it
State the combined impact plainly
items.explanation: The total cost is the point.

items.prompt: How should a pattern conversation end?
choices: With a warning of the consequences that follow
With a general hope for improvement over time
With one specific change and a date to look again
items.explanation: It keeps the goal as change.

items.prompt: Is 'over and over' a nameable Situation?
choices: No, it is not tied to any moment
Yes, it refers to many moments
Yes, because it is a repeated word
items.explanation: It names no instance.

items.prompt: A manager has seen the same gap in two standups and one planning call, but did not write down dates. What is the best next step?
choices: Recall and confirm each instance, or note the next one the same day
Say that it keeps happening and let the report supply the dates
Describe it as a long-standing habit when the review comes round
Give the feedback as a single trait so that nobody repeats mistakes
items.explanation: Each instance needs to be a nameable Situation, or the message is a trait again.
items.reference:
Pattern = dated instances
list each instance: when, what, cost
state combined impact plainly
ask what is in the way
agree one change and a date to look again
Why: a pattern is made of nameable Situations; adjectives like 'always' cannot be checked and start an argument about the word.
items.learnMore:
Building a pattern conversation

Waiting through several instances hoping the issue fades turns the eventual talk into accumulated criticism. Naming each instance keeps it a set of facts.

Common mistake

Saving up frustration and then saying 'this keeps happening.' It sounds like an accusation with nothing to check.
items.reflection: Is there a recurring thing you have been meaning to raise with someone? Can you name two dated instances?

items.prompt: Why does 'you always do this' lead to an argument about the wrong thing?
choices: It signals that the manager has already decided on a rating for them
It is usually spoken louder than other kinds of feedback are
One counterexample is easy to find, so the talk becomes about 'always'
It lacks a clear tone of real concern for the person involved
items.explanation: An unverifiable absolute is easy to dispute and shifts the topic away from the events.

items.prompt: If the impact was minor, the Impact part should...
choices: be exaggerated for effect
be left out completely
say so honestly
items.explanation: True size keeps trust.

items.prompt: Exaggerating impact mostly damages...
choices: the current meeting only
trust in future feedback
the company's budget
items.explanation: Once noticed, the next impact is discounted.

items.prompt: Feedback in front of the whole team should usually be...
choices: A named correction of one single person
General guidance about a team norm
A joke at the expense of the person
items.explanation: The person-specific talk stays private.

items.prompt: Where should the person-specific conversation happen?
choices: In private
In front of peers
In a company-wide email
items.explanation: Naming someone in public is public criticism.

items.prompt: Is public, specific praise usually fine?
choices: No, never, in any circumstance at all
Only in annual performance reviews
Yes, with the person's context in mind
items.explanation: Positive feedback does not carry the same risk.

items.prompt: A team-level version might say...
choices: 'Priya hid the delay on us again, as usual'
'Some of you are clearly not trying hard enough'
'Let's say flagged blockers out loud in standup'
items.explanation: It states the norm without naming one person.

items.prompt: If the impact is small, should the structure be skipped?
choices: No, keep it and size the Impact honestly
Yes, small things aren't worth the effort
Yes, but only when it is put in writing
items.explanation: Small does not mean absent.

items.prompt: What changes when the audience grows?
choices: The truth of the facts themselves
Who is named and how general it is
The need for specifics in what is said
items.explanation: Facts stay true; the framing adapts.

items.prompt: Nobody replanned anything; the missing update only made the week slightly less smooth. Which Impact line is right?
choices: It nearly derailed the sprint and could have cost us dearly in the end
There was no impact at all, so there is nothing here worth saying
It would have made the week a little smoother, nothing more
It shows a habit that will eventually harm the team's wider work
items.explanation: State the impact at its real size. Inflation and omission both fail.
items.reference:
Sizing the impact and the audience
small impact: say it at true size
team audience: generalize S and B, keep the person talk private
good news: public specific praise is usually fine
Why: exaggerated impact spends trust, and naming one person in front of peers turns private feedback into public criticism.
items.learnMore:
Impact size and audience

Honest sizing of the Impact keeps future high-stakes feedback believable. When the audience widens, the message becomes a team norm rather than a named correction.

Common mistake

Raising the stakes ('this could have sunk the project') to make a small point land. People notice, and discount the next one.
items.reflection: Think of a group message you've seen that was really about one person. What would the group-level version have said?

items.prompt: Why is inflating a small impact worse than omitting it?
choices: It plants a claim the receiver can disprove and discounts later true impact
It makes the feedback far too long for anyone to remember properly
It forces the manager to move to a formal and documented review cycle
It removes the Behavior from the message entirely, leaving only mood
items.explanation: Omission loses little; exaggeration spends credibility.
